Title: Lolita
Author: Vladimir Nabokov
Review: The writing is gorgeous which contrasts with the creepy subject matter in the most disturbing way. It’s strange but fascinating to be inside a criminal’s head. He knows what he’s doing is wrong and is manipulative throughout, more or less successfully. Dolores doesn’t ever get a voice. Every time she speaks and everything she does is filtered through an extremely unreliable and perverse narrator. Despite the fact that the reader spends the whole book inside his head, he never cares to find out what’s actually going on inside her head. This is an incredibly powerful book but anyone who thinks it’s in anyway a love story is a walking red flag.

Title: Jews, God and History
Author: Max I. Dimont
Review:
Was fascinating right up until the creation of Israel when it became largely propaganda, including the myth that Palestine was empty desert, that there’s no second class citizenship in Israel, and that Israel was trying to help the Palestinians who kept trying to terrorize them (the book ends in the late 80s). The author also uses words like Islamism and Mohammedans for some reason, although didn’t otherwise seem anti-Arab.

I also would have loved more chapters about the experiences of Jews in the Middle East and North Africa but it focused largely on Europe, though a couple Muslim empires were discussed briefly. The histories of idea of who the Jews are and what keeps them around, and even thriving, in diasporas in any number of countries, was particularly interesting.

(There were also a few moments of questionable historical accuracy, as when he claimed Israel was the world’s first democracy without explanation, but as it’s not the only book I’ve read or will read about the history of the Jews or the Middle East, this didn’t bother me much.)

Review: It's been many years since l've read any of Vanada Shiva's books and I shouldn't wait so long to read the next one. Her books are simultaneously infuriating and hopeful because she outlines the enormous damage free market capitalism has done to millions of people but also provides new ideas, new (or quite old, really) economic frameworks. The choice between capitalism and communism has never worked for me, mostly because neither of those systems has ever worked for a majority of people who are stuck within them. Old Indigenous systems, community-based and local systems, provide more intriguing options.

Review:
I wish there was an updated edition because this was so informative and easy to read. My main takeaways were that multinational corporations do an extraordinary amounts of harm, controlling the narrative takes a lot of money, and the law usually only applies to the poor. The rich are pretty-well exempt. Also, girls should be in school.

Alvarado is an impressive woman doing incredible work with almost no resources. Unfortunately, I don’t think the situation has improved a lot for the poor in Honduras since the 80s — the same companies still control most of the land and the US military is still doing US military things.

Review: I appreciate books like this for learning more about plants in my area (I’m getting much better at identifying a lot of them!) and I appreciate the considerable reference section. One thing I would have liked is if those references were connected to claims through the book so I knew where they came from. Another thing I would have loved is more specificity when it comes to claims about what Indigenous peoples have used certain plants for. For instance, I lost count of the number of times a sentence went like this: “Native tribes (sic) have traditionally used x plant for y purpose”. I kept wondering which First Nations and where that information came from. One last thing I did really like were the notes on endangered plants as well as poisonous ones so you know which ones to leave alone.

Title: Twilight of Democracy: The Seductive Lure of Authoritarianism
Author: Anne Applebaum
Review:
Interesting but seems to miss some perspectives. I’m not at all convinced that Howard Zinn and others who criticise the “myth of American exceptionalism” are anti-American so much as realists who recognise that things like slavery don’t make a country a “shining city on a hill”. I’m also not at all convinced by arguments about “identify politics” when some people, e.g. black Americans and trans people, are just fighting for their right to exist in some places.

I’m also not convinced that, amongst some anyway, there’s not a thread to follow between the politics of Reagan and the politics of Trump. Applebaum seems to approve of Reagan but doesn’t think there’s a relationship between his ideas and Trump’s. That said, I agree that some views, e.g. of Russia and democratic ideals, have changed dramatically since the Cold War.

Review:
Mostly very good but not for me.

A couple criticisms:

He’s also an example of why I’m hesitant to take an Englishman’s version of Irish or Scottish beliefs seriously. He conflates the Calleach, Nicneven, Hecate, and Baba Yaga as different versions of the “witch mother” which doesn’t seem at all reasonable to me. He also says that the Calleach transforms into Nicneven in the spring which I think is a myth he made up.

He also seems inclined to believe that women killed in the witch trials were actual witches and seems to believe their testimonies as true rather than things people said under torture to make it stop or under threat of death. Maybe some actually believed certain things but surely not all. I doubt most were even witches.

An incredible thought-provoking book full of all manner of challenging and interesting ideas. I’ll have to mull these over for a while and, probably, reread it some time. I’m not 100% convinced that the legal system can never provide justice (I guess that depends how you define justice), but it sure doesn’t seem to do that for women, trans people, or people of colour very often, so we definitely need better ideas.

(I’m in Canada but on the prairies our police originated to remove Indigenous people from their homes to make room for white settlers, so the situation is different than the American one but not better. Except for the for-profit prison thing. There currently aren’t any in Canada and there are many problems with Canadian prisons but making prisons for-profit seems like a magnet for unethical behavior and not on the part of the prisoners. And the death penalty.)

Review:
I loved a lot about The Cauldron and the Drum, and I'll definitely reread it. I'm always skeptical about the use of the word "shamanism" because it's so often misused and misunderstood and I don't think it was necessary to use in this context. Western words like "seership" for western practices work fine. I do feel more connected, culturally, to the idea of the three cauldrons rather than the chakra system(s), so I'll have to learn more about that. I also refer to this as Irish rather than Celtic practice because there's really no such thing as pan-Celticism, either in history or the present-day. Therefore, I look for cultural specificity when learning about either historical or modern practices.

Correction: it's sort of a thing and if Celtic people are into it, more power to them, but most often it's weird English romanticised notions of Celtic peoples.

This area of the world is criminally underrated in the west and I’m so glad a know a little bit more about it now.

Publisher: Flatiron Books: A Moment of Lift Book
Review: I enjoy any scientist’s enthusiasm and wonder around their subject and I’m glad she got into the ethics of AI, but I think it’s a bit unfortunate that that only happened in the last little section of the book. I think scientists have a social responsibility to imagine the uses of their creations by the tech billionaires because those billionaires have no sense of ethics or responsibility to anyone other than themselves and their shareholders and most politicians are no better. I know it’s hard because the technology is so cool in itself, but it’s also harming both people and the environment.

Title: James
Author: Percival Everett
Review: I love these sorts of anti-colonial responses to classic books and this is a fantastic take on Huck Finn. It’s been a while since I read that book, and there were some things that were not as I remembered, especially in regards to Huck’s early views on Jim as well as the ending, but overall this was a riveting story about a man who wanted to be treated like a man and not a slave and his journey (adventures?) to get there. I’ll have to try other books by this author.

Title: The Hunter (Cal Hooper, #2)
Author: Tana French
Review: The Hunter was not a typical mystery thriller by any stretch, but it was a captivating story. I was completely invested in the main characters. And I enjoyed the Irish dialogue—the audiobook narrator was excellent.

Title: The Book Censor's Library
Author: Bothayna Al-Essa
Review: I liked this one a lot. A little bit 1984, a little bit Fahrenheit 451, and a little bit Alice in Wonderland. We’re all mad here. And it’s slightly too believable in this era of increased book banning “to protect people”. If my personal library ever gets me into trouble, at least I’ll know where the little white rabbits come from. In the meantime, I’m off to read another book.

Title: The God of the Woods
Author: Liz    Moore
Review: The God of the Woods is called a thriller, but it isn’t. It’s more of a historical fiction mystery that moves quite slowly. It’s interesting but the rapid changes in several perspectives and timelines made it hard to get into because it was hard to keep things straight. A few of the characters are also hard to like in an obnoxious rich people sort of way but they’re also interesting, at least. If I liked the writing style more, I probably wouldn’t have minded in the slow pacing as much in the middle, but it was only okay for me.

Author: Kate J. Neville
Review: This gave me a lot to think about, in the best way. It got off to a slower start than some of the books I’ve read lately, so for a minute, I was thinking that I wanted it to pick up the pace, but actually, it was exactly the pace it needed to be. It’s a collection of essays that wonders about a variety of topics from environmentalism to economics through the lens of idleness and leisure vs productivity and what that might mean for our future on this funny little planet.

Don’t buy into the propaganda and censorship campaigns—they seem to be mostly lies anyway. I don’t want other people dictating what I am able to read based on their religious or political beliefs. Monitor your own kids (and their internet access). Censoring other people is never going to be the answer.

Review: There was a lot that I liked about the premise but the execution wasn’t as good as Weyward. The first two thirds were quite slow and hard to get into. The ending was better, at least.

Title: The Message
Author: Ta-Nehisi Coates
Review:
I always appreciate how thoughtful and unflinching Coates is. This is a blunt book on modern-day colonialism and the morality gymnastics people perform when determining who gets to be considered fully human and the consequences that are experienced when the oppressed become the oppressors.

I would have liked this book to be a bit longer with the ideas more developed, however, a lot of the negative reviews I’ve seen of this book being biased and not contextualised are themselves biased and not contextualised, and horribly conflate Hamas with all Palestinians.

Title: One Day, Everyone Will Have Always Been Against This

Review: Phenomenal, powerful writing. There’s really nothing in this book that isn’t easily available online, that anyone couldn’t figure out for themselves, but people in positions of power in the West can’t seem to handle truth dealt so bluntly. If the arc of the moral universe really does bend toward justice, it’s taken a dramatic wrong turn and this is a flashing neon sign pointing that out. I hope some people will listen, but I’m not really convinced that they will.

Author: John Fugelsang
Review: I tend to prefer books like The Bible Says So by Dan McClellen but I’m not entirely sure I’m the target audience for this one as a leftist Canadian! I did grow up with people who chose a religion of hate and I’m not convinced that all these arguments will convince them, but maybe some are worth a try. For instance, the idea that the extremists would be against gay marriage but not straight divorce is inaccurate,l; in my experience, the extremists I know are against both. Basically, I’m not entirely sure what to make of this book but I hope it can help some people.
